processing: The flowers, sometimes with the upper herb, are dried without further processing.
harvest_season: The plant flowers from early summer to early autumn, and the creamy-white flower clusters are the part usually dried for tea.
appearance_dry: Crumbly cream-to-pale-yellow flower heads mixed with bits of green stem.
appearance_wet: Soft, faded cream florets with limp green fragments.
taste_profile: One tea-maker's account says the tea does not taste very good and differs from the flower lemonade, which tastes of almond or amaretto. Expect a light herbal cup that may turn bitter.

brewing.notes: About 2 teaspoons of dried flowers per 250 ml of boiling water, steeped 10 minutes. The plant contains salicin, so people sensitive to aspirin or on blood thinners should ask a doctor first.

vintage_note: Sold as a dried herb with no vintage, loose or in bags. As with other dried flowers, the current year's summer gathering smells best, and aroma is what you are paying for, so judge it by smell.
description:
Meadowsweet is a tall perennial of damp meadows across Europe and Western Asia, with frothy creamy flowers and a very strong sweet smell. As a tea it is all about that scent.

The flowers are simply dried, so there is little to say about processing and a lot to say about freshness.

The smell promises more than the cup delivers. One tea-maker's account finds the tea not very tasty and prefers the flowers in a lemonade, which tastes of almond or amaretto.

The plant contains salicin and is called a natural aspirin, so anyone sensitive to aspirin should ask a doctor first. Buy it from a seller who can tell you what plant it is, since the Russian names таволга and лабазник both circulate for it.
history:
The English name dates from the 16th century and first meant a plant for flavouring mead, with the older form meadsweet going back to the 15th century. Chaucer's The Knight's Tale calls it meadwort, an ingredient in a drink called save.

It was also strewn in churches for festivals and weddings, which earned it the name bridewort. In Russian and wider European folk medicine, the herb, flowers and roots have long been used in infusions and decoctions, and the plant appears in several Western European pharmacopoeias.
